techniques.name: GNNExplainer
techniques.description: GNNExplainer explains one prediction of a graph neural network, a model that passes information along the edges of a graph such as a molecule, a payment network or a mesh of weather grid points, by finding a small subgraph and a small set of input features that most support that prediction. Explanation methods for flat inputs, such as SHAP and LIME, give each input feature its own score and have no built-in notion of a connection between two nodes; this method scores the connections themselves, restricted to the part of the graph the model actually reads for the prediction (its computation graph, the neighbourhood within as many hops as the model has message-passing layers). It learns a mask with a value between 0 and 1 for each edge of that computation graph and for each node-feature dimension by gradient descent: the masked graph is fed to the model, and the masks are adjusted to keep the predicted label as likely as possible while penalties keep the total mask small and push values towards 0 or 1. Edges and features whose mask values fall below a threshold are then dropped, leaving a compact subgraph and feature subset that can be drawn over the input graph; the same procedure explains node labels, predicted links and whole-graph labels, and the original paper also aligns the explanations of many nodes of one class into a summary pattern. It needs gradient access to the model, and each explanation is a separate optimisation.

example_use_cases.description: A pharmaceutical company's computational toxicology team uses a graph neural network to flag candidate molecules as likely mutagenic. For each flagged compound it reviews the substructure and atom features GNNExplainer selects and checks them against known structural alerts such as nitro groups, to decide whether a flag rests on chemistry the team recognises before the compound is deprioritised.

A bank's financial-crime unit scores accounts with a graph neural network over its payment network to flag likely money-mule accounts. Investigators receive with each flag the explanation subgraph of counterparties and transfers and the account features it selected, and use them to decide whether to escalate; model validators sample explanations to check that flags do not rest mainly on features such as branch or account-opening channel.

A weather service's model evaluation team runs the regression mode of the PyTorch Geometric implementation on a small set of high-impact forecasts from a graph-based forecasting model, such as the predicted rainfall total at one location. Forecasters check whether the connections and input variables selected, for example humidity upwind, are physically plausible, and the team deletes the selected connections to confirm the forecast changes, before such forecasts feed a warning service.

limitations.description: Each explanation is a separate optimisation, run for a set number of steps (100 by default in the PyTorch Geometric implementation), so explaining many nodes or graphs is slow and explanations of similar cases are not required to agree. A view of the model as a whole needs an extra step, such as the class-level summary in the original paper, or a method that trains one explainer for all instances.

The masks are soft during optimisation, so the model is run on graphs whose edges and features are scaled by fractions it never saw in training, and these values can add meaning or noise of their own. The objective is not convex and the masks start at random: in a 2024 benchmark, the ten-edge explanations from runs with different seeds overlapped by a Jaccard index of only 0.18 to 0.80 across six datasets. The final subgraph also depends on the threshold used to cut the mask.

The size of the explanation is set by the user, not found. The original experiments fixed it at the known size of the planted pattern on synthetic graphs and at 10 edges and 5 features on real ones, and the PyTorch Geometric implementation advises tuning the size penalty to the graph's average degree. A compact explanation can therefore leave out structure the model uses.

Most evidence that it finds the right structure comes from synthetic graphs with planted patterns, and a trained model need not use the planted edges, so agreement with them can mislead. A 2023 benchmark found graph explainers, this one included, less faithful when linked nodes tend to differ and when the deciding structure is large. Check fidelity on your own model, for example by deleting the explanation and measuring the change.

It assumes the computation graph is small. The computation graph grows with every message-passing layer, so in a mesh-based forecasting model that passes messages many times along long-range edges (GraphCast uses 16 such layers) it probably spans most of the mesh: the mask then covers most edges and compactness comes from the size penalty, not the model. This has not been tested. PyTorch Geometric applies the mask inside its own message-passing layers, so the model must use them or be adapted.

resources.title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
resources.abstract:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a powerful tool for machine learning on graphs.GNNs combine node feature information with the graph structure by 
recursively passing neural messages along edges of the input graph. However, incorporating both graph structure and feature information leads to complex models,
and explaining predictions made by GNNs remains unsolved. Here
we propose GNNExplainer, the first general, model-agnostic approach for providing interpretable explanations for predictions of any GNN-based model on any graph-based machine learning task. Given an instance, GNNExplainer identifies a compact subgraph structure and a small subset of node features that have a crucial role in GNN's prediction. 
Further, GNNExplainer  can generate consistent and concise explanations for an entire class of instances.
We formulate GNNExplainer as an optimization task that maximizes the mutual information between a GNN's prediction and distribution of possible subgraph structures. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs show that our approach can identify important graph structures as well as node features, and outperforms baselines by 17.1% on average. GNNExplainer  provides a variety of benefits, from the ability to visualize semantically relevant structures to interpretability, to giving insights into errors of faulty GNNs.

techniques.name: TimeSHAP
techniques.description: TimeSHAP explains one prediction of a model that reads a sequence of events, such as a recurrent neural network that scores a bank transaction using the account's history, by giving each past event, each input feature and selected event-feature cells a Shapley value: a share of the score, taken from cooperative game theory, such that all the shares add up to the difference between the model's score and its score with every event and feature removed. It adapts KernelSHAP, the sampling estimator in SHAP, which explains a single input vector and so, applied to the latest event of a recurrent model, gives earlier events no credit; TimeSHAP instead switches off whole rows or columns of the event-by-feature input matrix, replacing them with a background value (the training-data average in the original paper), queries the model on many such perturbed sequences, and fits a weighted linear model whose coefficients are the attributions. Because the number of event combinations doubles with every event, a pruning step first walks back from the most recent event and merges all older events into a single player once their combined attribution falls below a chosen tolerance, and cell-level values are computed only where the most important events and features intersect, with the other cells grouped. The model is treated as a black box that takes a batch of sequences and returns one score per sequence, and the output is event, feature and cell attributions for each explained sequence, plus plots that aggregate them across many sequences into a global view.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's fraud operations team runs TimeSHAP on each alert from its recurrent account-takeover model, so the analyst reviewing an alert sees which earlier events (for example a password change, then a login from a new device) and which features carried the score, not only the payment being held. The analyst uses this to decide whether to release the payment or contact the customer, and the model team samples the explanations to check that the drivers match known fraud patterns.

A hospital data-science team validating a recurrent model that predicts next-day escalation of treatment for patients in intensive care computes event- and feature-level TimeSHAP values for test-set patients and reviews them with clinicians. Drivers the clinicians judge implausible, such as an indicator that a measurement is missing outweighing the measurements themselves, are investigated before the model is used in a prospective study.

An airport's forecasting team using a recurrent model to warn of fog in the next six hours from the past 48 hours of station observations uses the pruning statistics and global event plots to find how far back the model actually draws on, and the feature attributions to check that humidity, temperature and wind lead each warning. The findings set the input window for the next retraining and go into the model's validation report.

limitations.description: Every attribution is measured against the background chosen to stand for a removed event or feature, the training-data average in the original paper. A sequence containing averaged events may be unlike anything the model has seen, and another background gives other attributions; the original authors note that a feature scoring zero for every sequence may reflect the background rather than the model. Report the background with the results.

Exact values need every combination of events, which doubles with each event. On the original fraud data (median sequence about 138 events), exact values were possible for only 10% of sequences with 32,000 sampled combinations, and repeated runs disagreed (relative standard deviation 1.71 without pruning, 0.98 at the chosen tolerance). With tens of thousands of model calls per explanation, explaining every scored event in real time is impractical; the alerts people review are the usual scope.

Pruning trades detail on older events for speed and stability. All events before the cut-off share one attribution. The cut-off test compares the older block's net, signed attribution with a user-set tolerance, so by construction an early event that pushed the score up can pass unseen if others pushed it down; the original paper does not measure how often this happens. Results change with the tolerance, so fix it in advance and report it.

It explains one score per sequence: the reference implementation expects the model to return a single value for each sequence. A model with many outputs, such as a forecast for several lead times or locations, needs a separate run or a chosen summary for each. The attributions show what the model relies on, not causes in the world: in the original study a high attribution to customer age led to a bias audit, which was needed to establish the disparity.

Each event and feature receives one number, so an effect that arises only from a combination, such as a settings change followed by a login from a new device, is shared out among its parts: an analyst sees each part with some credit but cannot tell that they matter only together. Cell-level values are computed only where the top-ranked events and features intersect. A clinical study using the method found escalation effects hard to see and suggested interactions as the cause.

techniques.name: Appropriate Reliance Measurement
techniques.description: Appropriate reliance measurement tests whether people who receive an AI system's advice follow it when it is right and keep their own judgement when it is wrong, and whether an explanation, or another aid such as a confidence score, moves them towards that pattern. It uses a two-step decision study on a classification task, the only kind Schemmer et al. define it for: for each task item the participant first decides alone, then sees the AI's advice, with or without the explanation, and makes a final decision, on a set of items with known correct answers drawn so that the AI is wrong on a known share of them. Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree are counted, because when they agree the final decision cannot show which source the person relied on. Schemmer et al. define two rates over these items: relative AI reliance, the share of items with a wrong first decision and correct advice on which the person switched to the advice, and relative self-reliance, the share of items with a correct first decision and wrong advice on which the person kept their own answer. Comparing the two rates between an explanation condition and a control condition shows whether the explanation reduces under-reliance (rejecting correct advice), reduces over-reliance (accepting wrong advice) or merely raises agreement with the AI, which overall accuracy or agreement with the AI does not show on its own.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer considering highlighted claim features as an explanation for its fraud-flagging model runs a two-step study with its claims handlers on 40 past claims, with the model wrong on a quarter of them, comparing handlers who see the flag alone with handlers who also see the highlights. It adopts the highlights only if relative AI reliance rises without relative self-reliance falling, since higher acceptance of all advice, right and wrong, would show deference rather than better judgement.

A conservation charity whose volunteers identify bird species with help from an image classifier measures relative AI reliance and relative self-reliance separately for experienced birders and beginners, and for example-based and written explanations. It chooses which explanation to show each group from the results, because a volunteer's expertise changes how an explanation, especially a wrong one, shifts their reliance on the classifier.

A hospital whose safety case for a sepsis alert relies on ward doctors overriding wrong alerts, and whose workflow has doctors record their own escalation decision before the alert appears, runs a vignette study in that workflow, with and without the alert's explanation panel. Before switching the panel on, it reports relative self-reliance, and the share of wrong-alert cases that ended in a wrong decision, against the oversight requirement in the safety case.

limitations.description: The rates describe behaviour on a task set built to contain many AI errors: Schemmer et al. drew equal numbers of items from each cell of the confusion matrix, which put the AI's accuracy on their 16 items at 50%. The study does not show how people rely on advice when errors are rarer, as they usually are in service, so it supports a claim about the conditions tested, not a direct estimate of over-reliance in deployment.

Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree enter the two rates, so each rate can rest on a handful of items per person, and items on which the person and the AI are wrong together, the errors that oversight cannot catch, enter neither rate. Plan the sample around the expected number of disagreements, and report beside the rates the share of wrong-advice items that ended in a wrong final decision.

Asking for a decision before the advice is shown is itself an intervention. Guo et al.'s reanalysis of an earlier study found reliance closer to the appropriate level when people decided first than when they saw the AI's advice first, so a two-step study may show better reliance than a deployed system that presents the advice straight away.

The rates judge each decision by whether the advice turned out to be right, not by whether following it was the better bet given what the person could see. Guo et al. argue that this outcome-based definition mixes two failures, wrong beliefs about how often the AI is right and poor use of those beliefs, and treats a close call the same as an obvious one, so a low rate does not say which to fix.

Results depend on who takes part and on how good the explanations are. Morrison et al. found that participants' expertise changed how incorrect explanations affected their reliance, and that example-based explanations misled participants more than written ones, so a result from novices, or from explanations that were always correct, does not carry over to expert users or to explanations that are sometimes wrong.

techniques.name: Think-Aloud Study of Explanation Use
techniques.description: A think-aloud study of explanation use asks a small number of participants to say what they are thinking while they use an AI system's explanations to do a realistic task, so that the design team can see how the explanation is read, used, ignored or misread. It applies the think-aloud method from cognitive psychology, which rests on Ericsson and Simon's account of verbal reports: people can voice what they are attending to as they work without changing their thinking, provided they are not asked to report things they would not otherwise attend to, such as the reasons for their actions. In a session, a facilitator gives a short practice task, then sets tasks in which the participant sees the model's output and explanation and makes a decision, and while the participant works gives only neutral reminders, such as 'what are you thinking?', when they fall silent; audio and screen are recorded. The recordings are transcribed and coded, often by thematic analysis, into findings such as parts of the explanation that were misread, parts never looked at and questions it left unanswered, and the team changes the design and tests it again. The output is qualitative, design-stage evidence about how an explanation is understood: it can show that a misreading occurs, but not how often it occurs among users or whether their decisions improve.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a nurse-facing explanation for a patient deterioration score runs think-aloud sessions with six ward nurses on a clickable prototype using past patient records. It finds that nurses read a factor that lowered the score as a sign that the patient was improving, relabels the chart, and re-tests the new labels in a second round before fixing the design for a quantitative evaluation.

The developer of a vocal emotion-recognition app that highlights which parts of a recording drove each prediction runs remote think-aloud sessions with a dozen users. One participant reads the highlight colour bar as a trace of the speaker's tone of voice, a misreading that no rating of the explanation would have revealed, and the team changes how the highlight is drawn.

A bank's model risk team preparing to give loan officers counterfactual explanations (for example, the income at which a refused application would have been approved) runs think-aloud sessions with five officers on past applications, including some the model got wrong. It learns which suggestions officers would pass on to applicants and which they reject as implausible, and decides whether to filter the suggestions before release.

limitations.description: How participants are asked to talk changes what is observed. A meta-analysis of 94 studies by Fox, Ericsson and Best found that plain thinking aloud left accuracy unchanged, but that asking people to explain or describe their thinking changed performance, and that verbal reports of every kind tended to make tasks take longer. Facilitators must avoid 'why' prompts, and task times from these sessions cannot serve as performance measures.

Talking through a task can make people attend to an explanation more than they would at work. In Buçinca et al.'s think-aloud study, participants' preferences between two explanation types matched the results of a proxy task rather than those of the realistic task, and the authors suggest thinking aloud pushed people into analytical thinking, so these sessions may overstate how closely users read explanations in normal use.

Studies use few participants (between 4 and 14 in the sources for this record), so a finding shows that a problem exists, not how common it is, and cannot support a claim about the share of users who understand an explanation or about decision quality. The sessions also show only the situations their tasks include: tasks need some wrong model outputs if the team wants to see how people use an explanation when the model errs.

Not everything people do with an explanation gets said. Quick, perceptual uses leave little trace: in Zhang and Lim's study, participants called the audio examples intuitive but did not say why they found them simple. People also tend to say what they think the right answer is, the social desirability bias the GOV.UK guidance warns of. Silence about part of an explanation does not mean it went unused or was understood, and a screen recording or gaze data is needed to tell these apart.

Findings depend on the analyst: coding transcripts into themes is interpretive, so a study meant to support an assurance claim needs a stated coding scheme and a second coder. The voice and screen recordings are personal data that need participants' consent and controlled storage, and recordings made on real cases may also hold personal data about the people those cases concern.

techniques.name: Conditional Demographic Disparity
techniques.description: Conditional demographic disparity (CDD) measures whether members of a protected group make up a larger share of the people a system turns down than of the people it accepts, after taking into account a factor that differs between groups and that the assessor treats as a legitimate explanation of outcomes; Wachter, Mittelstadt and Russell (2021) propose it as baseline statistical evidence for assessing possible discrimination under EU non-discrimination law. Demographic disparity is the group's share of the unfavourable outcomes minus its share of the favourable ones: in the Berkeley graduate admissions data the paper revisits, women were 46 per cent of rejected applicants but 32 per cent of admitted ones, a disparity of 0.14. CDD computes the same difference separately within each stratum of the conditioning attribute (there, the department applied to) and averages the strata, weighting each by its number of people, so a gap that arises only because groups apply in different proportions to strata with different acceptance rates (an instance of Simpson's paradox) drops out, while a gap within strata remains. Conditioning on department turns the Berkeley figure to about -0.02, a slight disparity in women's favour: within departments, women were on average 40 per cent of rejected and 42 per cent of admitted applicants. The output is the disparity in each stratum and their weighted average, computed on the outcomes recorded in a dataset before training or on a model's decisions after it; the authors present it as a descriptive magnitude to support a contextual judgement, not a pass-or-fail test, and the choice of conditioning attribute is a judgement the measure does not make.

example_use_cases.description: An employer's HR analytics team audits a CV-screening model used across job families. Women make up a larger share of screened-out applicants than of shortlisted ones overall, but apply in greater numbers to the families with the fewest vacancies per applicant, so the team reports CDD conditioned on job family, with each family's own disparity, letting the recruitment board see whether a gap remains within families before it decides whether to keep using the model.

A consumer lender's compliance team computes CDD on its credit model's decisions for applicants of different ethnic origins, recorded for equality monitoring, conditioned first on the loan product applied for and then on income band. It reports both results with the per-stratum figures and a written reason for treating each factor as a legitimate explanation, as the starting point for its assessment of possible indirect discrimination.

A local authority planning to train a model on past housing allocation decisions measures CDD in those decisions, conditioned on assessed band of housing need, before any training. A positive disparity for one ethnic group within need bands, larger than chance would explain, indicates that the labels carry a pattern a model could learn, and the project board uses the finding to decide whether those decisions can serve as training labels at all.

limitations.description: The result depends on which attribute is conditioned on, and the measure cannot tell whether that attribute is a legitimate explanation. If the attribute is itself shaped by discrimination, for instance if one group was deterred from applying to some departments, conditioning on it removes the very disparity a claimant would point to. Wachter et al. leave the choice of factors to courts and context, so each choice needs a recorded justification that a reviewer can contest.

The weighted average can hide large disparities of opposite sign in different strata. In the Berkeley data the per-department disparities run from about -0.09 to +0.05 around a summary of -0.02, and Wachter et al. note that the largest swings come from the department where few women applied, which chance alone could produce. A claim should rest on the per-stratum figures, with their counts, as well as on the summary.

Searching many conditioning attributes or their combinations will find disparities by chance, as the authors warn, and choosing among them after seeing the results can equally make a real one disappear. The authors also offer a descriptive magnitude rather than a statistical test, and set no threshold for how much disparity is too much, so the conditioning attributes need fixing before the data are examined, and a claim that a gap is real needs an interval or test added.

CDD compares shares of outcomes, not rates, so the same gap in acceptance rates gives a smaller value where the group is a small part of a stratum: accepted at 20 per cent against 50 per cent for others, a group scores about 0.33 where it is half the stratum but 0.02 where it is 2 per cent. A fixed threshold therefore tolerates larger rate gaps for smaller groups. Scores and graded outcomes must also first be cut into favourable and unfavourable, and the result changes with the cut.

In the open-source SageMaker Clarify code, a stratum where everyone gets the same outcome is counted rather than skipped: an all-rejected stratum adds a disparity equal to the group's share of it, though no one there was treated differently, so such strata need removing first. AWS has closed Clarify to new customers. The calculation is easy to reimplement, but published applications to deployed AI systems are scarce; the paper's worked example is the 1975 Berkeley admissions study.

techniques.name: Disaggregated Evaluation
techniques.description: Disaggregated evaluation assesses and reports a system's performance separately for each group of people a claim covers, and for combinations of groups (intersectional groups, such as darker-skinned women), so that a good overall score cannot hide a group for whom the system works badly. Following Barocas et al. (2021), the evaluator first fixes the design choices that change what the evaluation can show: which groups and combinations to report; how other factors that affect performance, such as lighting or recording conditions, are handled (held constant, varied deliberately, or left as they occur); which metrics to use, for a classifier often false positive and false negative rates reported separately, because each can harm different people; and whether the evaluation is exploratory, or confirmatory, meaning that it tests hypotheses stated in advance on data built to hold enough cases in every group. Each metric is then computed on a labelled evaluation set for every group and combination, together with the number of cases behind it and an interval showing how far the estimate could move through sampling alone, obtained for example by resampling the evaluation set. Groups are compared by absolute and by relative gaps, which can tell different stories: false negative rates of 1 and 10 per cent differ by nine points but tenfold. The output is a table or chart of per-group and per-combination results with their case counts and intervals, and a record of the design choices needed to interpret them; it is this design, more than any one metric or interval method, that decides which comparisons the evaluation can support and how conclusive each is.

example_use_cases.description: Before a hospital trust adopts a supplier's skin-lesion classifier, its clinical safety team reports sensitivity and specificity on locally labelled images for each skin-tone group, sex and age band, and for skin tone crossed with sex. Cells holding fewer melanoma cases than the evaluation protocol requires are marked as too small to estimate rather than reported, and the trust collects more images for them before deciding whether the tool may be used for all patients.

A consumer organisation evaluating the speech-to-text services behind automated phone lines has speakers from several regional and ethnic groups, matched on age and gender, read identical scripted passages, and reports word error rate per group with intervals. Because everyone says the same words, a gap can be attributed to how each service recognises speech rather than to what was said, the evidence the organisation needs for a complaint to the providers.

A bank's model risk team runs a confirmatory evaluation of its fraud model each quarter. The groups (age band, sex and their combinations), the metrics (false positive rate, which drives blocked legitimate payments, and false negative rate), the sample and the largest acceptable gap are fixed in a protocol before the data are drawn, and the model stays in service only if every interval for a gap lies inside that margin.

An exam board piloting an automated essay-scoring model runs an exploratory evaluation of its agreement with human markers, split by first language, school type and their combinations. It finds one weak cell, candidates with English as an additional language at small schools, too small to be conclusive, and commissions a confirmatory study with a sample built to fill that cell before deciding whether the scores can count towards grades.

limitations.description: Each attribute added multiplies the number of cells and shrinks each one, so combinations of attributes soon hold too few cases for a stable estimate, and where a cell holds only a few errors, intervals from resampling come out too narrow. Comparing many cells also throws up some large gaps by chance. A confirmatory claim needs enough cases in every cell, which Barocas et al. note existing datasets rarely provide, so the data available limit which comparisons can be tested.

A gap between groups shows that performance differs, not why. Another factor that affects performance may differ between the groups, as with the time between paired images that NIST suggested could explain a higher false negative rate for Asian people in face recognition. Holding such a factor constant hides gaps at its other values, varying it needs the factor labelled for every case, and strongly correlated factors are hard to separate, or impossible when they always occur together.

The result is only as good as two sets of labels. Where ground-truth outcomes are wrong, or recorded differently for different groups, and the extent of the error cannot be identified, Barocas et al. note the results are meaningless however careful the design. Group membership is often ascribed by an institution or inferred from appearance, adding errors and possible harm to those labelled, and datasets may hold few of some groups (darker-skinned women were 4.4 per cent of one benchmark).

It measures differences in performance and nothing else. Equal error rates say nothing about whether outputs stereotype or demean people, or whether favourable decisions are shared in proportion, and narrowing a gap under one metric can open a gap under another. A clean result supports a claim about the performance gaps measured, for the groups and conditions tested, and no wider fairness claim.

Results on a laboratory dataset may not carry over to the system in use, where lighting, recording conditions and operators' decisions differ, and Barocas et al. note that a component's performance alone may say little about the whole system around it. Evaluating in the setting of use captures this but is costly, and is often impossible for an outside evaluator, who usually sees the system only as a black box.

resources.abstract: Recent studies demonstrate that machine learning algorithms can discriminate based on classes like race and gender. In this work, we present an approach to evaluate bias present in automated facial analysis algorithms and datasets with respect to phenotypic subgroups. Using the dermatologist  approved Fitzpatrick Skin Type classification system, we characterize the gender and skin type distribution of two facial analysis benchmarks, IJB-A and Adience. We find that these datasets are overwhelmingly composed of lighter-skinned subjects (79.6% for IJB-A and 86.2% for Adience) and introduce a new facial analysis dataset which is balanced by gender and skin type. We evaluate 3 commercial gender classification systems using our dataset and show that darker-skinned females are the most misclassified group (with error rates of up to 34.7%). The maximum error rate for lighter-skinned males is 0.8%. The substantial disparities in the accuracy of classifying darker females, lighter females, darker males, and lighter males in gender classification systems require urgent attention if commercial companies are to build genuinely fair, transparent and accountable facial analysis algorithms.

techniques.name: Predictive Parity and Calibration Within Groups
techniques.description: This test checks whether a model's output means the same for every group: among people who receive the same score or the same decision, the share who turn out to have the outcome (or its average, for an outcome such as a cost or a count of illnesses) should not depend on their group, a requirement the fairness literature calls sufficiency. For a model that outputs a risk score, cases with known outcomes are grouped into score bins and, for each group, the observed outcome rate in each bin is plotted against the score, giving one calibration curve per group (a score is calibrated when, of the cases scored 0.3, about 30 per cent have the outcome); calibration within groups (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan) holds when each group's curve matches the scores, and the weaker condition that the curves coincide holds when a given score corresponds to the same outcome rate in every group. For a yes/no decision the same comparison is made in the two cells of the decision: predictive parity (Chouldechova) holds when the positive predictive value, the share of people flagged positive who turn out positive, is equal across groups, and the negative predictive value can be compared in the same way for those not flagged. The two read-outs can disagree, because a score that means the same for every group can still give unequal positive predictive values at a threshold when the groups' scores are spread differently above it, so the test reports the read-out matching the output on which decisions are taken, with intervals and the gaps between groups. Where comparisons of error rates condition on the true outcome and ask whether people who turn out the same are treated the same, this test conditions on the model's output and asks whether people treated the same turn out the same; when the outcome is more common in one group, the two cannot both hold except in special cases.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team checks a deterioration-risk score before it is shown to ward staff. On a year of admissions with recorded outcomes it plots a calibration curve, with intervals, for each ethnic group and each sex, and approves the score for use with every patient only if, across the scores that trigger escalation, each group's curve stays within a band agreed with clinicians.

A lender's model validation team compares the repayment rate among approved applicants across age bands, using two years of outcomes, to check whether approval means the same for each band. Because a difference among the approved can come from how scores are spread above the cut-off rather than from a different bar for one band, it also compares the calibration curves of the underlying score before raising any finding with the credit risk committee.

A probation service assessing a supplier's reoffending-risk tool is shown evidence that its positive predictive value is equal across ethnic groups. Its analysts reproduce the figures on local data and set them beside the groups' false positive and false negative rates, which differ because reconviction rates differ, so that the oversight board chooses which criterion the tool will be held to with both sets of figures in front of it.

A health insurer auditing a score that selects members for a care-management programme checks twice whether the score means the same for every racial group: against next year's costs, the label the model was trained on, and against a measure of illness such as the number of active chronic conditions. A score calibrated for cost but not for illness, with one group sicker than another at the same score, would lead the insurer to retrain on a different label.

limitations.description: When the outcome is more common in one group, a score or decision that satisfies predictive parity cannot also give the groups both equal false positive and equal false negative rates, and calibration within groups cannot coexist with equal average scores for each group's positives and negatives except with perfect prediction or equal base rates (Chouldechova; Kleinberg et al.). Passing this test therefore means accepting unequal error rates, a choice the test informs but cannot make.

Passing says little about how accurately the model predicts for each group. A well-fitted model usually comes close to calibration within groups without any fairness intervention when group membership can be inferred from its inputs, and a model that predicts accurately for one group while giving everyone in another group that group's average rate is still perfectly calibrated (Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan). The result needs pairing with performance measured for each group.

The test uses recorded outcomes, so it inherits any difference between groups in how the outcome is recorded. Rearrest stands in for reoffending, and a care-management score was calibrated by race for health costs while, at the 97th percentile of the score, Black patients had 26 per cent more chronic illnesses than white patients (Obermeyer et al.). A model can pass while scoring one group's need too low, so the outcome tested must be the one the claim is about.

A gap in positive predictive value is not by itself evidence that the score treats groups differently: the value averages over everyone above the threshold, so it depends on how each group's scores are spread there and moves when the threshold moves. Chouldechova notes that well-calibrated scores can fail predictive parity, and the converse also holds. Where scores are available the calibration curves should be reported, and the threshold stated.

Per-group calibration curves need labelled cases across the score range in every group; in a small group the high-score bins may hold a handful of people, so their rates swing widely, and the choice of bin widths changes the picture. An outside auditor who sees only decisions, not scores, can test predictive parity but not calibration, so access determines which claim the evidence can support.

resources.abstract: Malnutrition is a frequently underdiagnosed condition leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. The Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS) deployed a machine learning model (MUST-Plus) to detect malnutrition upon hospital admission. However, in diverse patient groups, a poorly calibrated model may lead to misdiagnosis, exacerbating health care disparities. We explored the model’s calibration across different variables and methods to improve calibration. Data from adult patients admitted to five MSHS hospitals from January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, were analyzed. We compared MUST-Plus prediction to the registered dietitian’s formal assessment. Hierarchical calibration was assessed and compared between the recalibration sample (N = 49,562) of patients admitted between January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, and the hold-out sample (N = 17,278) of patients admitted between January 1, 2023 - September 30, 2023. Statistical differences in calibration metrics were tested using bootstrapping with replacement. Before recalibration, the overall model calibration intercept was −1.17 (95% CI: −1.20, −1.14), slope was 1.37 (95% CI: 1.34, 1.40), and Brier score was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.25, 0.26). Both weak and moderate measures of calibration were significantly different between White and Black patients and between male and female patients. Logistic recalibration significantly improved calibration of the model across race and gender in the hold-out sample. The original MUST-Plus model showed significant differences in calibration between White vs. Black patients. It also overestimated malnutrition in females compared to males. Logistic recalibration effectively reduced miscalibration across all patient subgroups. Continual monitoring and timely recalibration can improve model accuracy.

techniques.name: Rich Subgroup Fairness Auditing
techniques.description: Rich subgroup fairness auditing checks whether a binary classifier treats any subgroup much better or much worse than the population as a whole, where the subgroups are not a short list chosen in advance but every group that rules of a chosen kind over several protected attributes can describe, such as everyone for whom a weighted sum of age, sex and ethnicity indicators exceeds a threshold. Kearns, Neel, Roth and Wu (2018) proposed it to detect what they call fairness gerrymandering: a classifier can have equal false positive rates for men and for women, and for each ethnic group, yet very unequal rates for particular combinations, such as women of one ethnicity. For a chosen rate (the false positive or false negative rate, or in the paper also the rate of positive decisions), each subgroup is scored by the gap between its rate and the overall rate multiplied by the share of all records that are in the subgroup and count towards that rate (for the false positive rate, those with a negative true outcome), so a gap counts for more the larger the group, and the audit searches for the subgroup with the highest score. Exact search is computationally hard in the worst case, so it is posed as a weighted (cost-sensitive) classification problem over the protected attributes and solved approximately: the reference implementation fits two linear regressions that propose a candidate worst subgroup as a linear threshold rule, using only those attributes, the true outcomes and the classifier's decisions, not the model itself. The output is that rule with the subgroup's size, rate and weighted gap (called gamma), compared with a limit set beforehand; unlike reporting metrics for groups listed in advance, the audit finds subgroups nobody listed, and unlike multiaccuracy boosting, which checks a score's average error in each subgroup and then corrects the model, it compares a decision rate with the overall rate and changes nothing.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model risk team validating a credit-risk model before release audits its decisions on a held-out sample of past applicants whose repayment is known, and records that these are only applicants the old policy approved. It searches subgroups over age, sex, ethnicity and disability status for the worst false positive rate gap (good payers flagged as high risk), compares it with a limit agreed with the risk committee, and sends the rule for any subgroup over it to the developers.

A hospital's clinical AI team has confirmed that a sepsis early-warning model misses cases at similar rates for men and women and for each recorded ethnic group. Before rollout it audits the false negative rate over subgroups combining age, sex and ethnicity and, because the search is approximate, also scores a grid of rules over two of the attributes by brute force, as the method's authors did, to check the search did not miss a larger gap.

A local authority's internal audit team re-audits a model that flags housing benefit claims for fraud review each quarter, using a random sample of claims reviewed whether or not they were flagged. It records the worst subgroup by false positive rate (legitimate claims flagged) over age, sex, ethnicity and disability, with its size and gap, and escalates to the system owner when the weighted gap exceeds the agreed limit.

limitations.description: Finding the worst subgroup exactly is hard in the worst case, even for conjunctions or linear thresholds of attributes (Kearns et al. 2018, Theorem 3.3), so practical audits use a heuristic search. A subgroup it reports does have the measured gap on the audit data, but a clean result is only a lower bound: the authors note their auditor could miss a larger disparity and checked it by brute force on two attributes (Kearns et al. 2019). 'Nothing found' is a search result, not a proof.

Gaps are weighted by subgroup size, which the authors require for reliable estimates and which lets small groups pass with large gaps: a subgroup holding 2% of the records whose false positive rate is 20 percentage points above the overall rate scores at most 0.004, under the 0.005 limit used in the AIF360 demonstration. The audit cannot support a claim about a small named group; report that group's own rate, with an interval, instead.

Only subgroups that the rule class can describe, over the attributes designated as protected, are searched; the reference implementation uses linear threshold rules. The class has to be limited because, as the authors note, any imperfect classifier could be accused of unfairness to the set of people it misclassifies. A protected attribute that is not recorded or not designated is invisible, so the attributes used and their encoding must be stated with the finding.

Error-rate audits need the protected attributes and the true outcome for every audited record, which a deployed system may not supply, for example when outcomes are seen only for approved applications. Reliable estimates need more data the richer the subgroup class, the authors' experiments report in-sample results, and the tools give no confidence interval, so audit on held-out data and repeat on fresh data before relying on a worst-case figure.

It tests parity of one rate at a time for binary decisions, each subgroup's rate against the overall rate. A pass on false positives says nothing about false negatives, the AIF360 auditor implements only those two error rates, and other criteria, such as whether scores mean the same in every subgroup (calibration), need a different test. The rate must be chosen to match the fairness claim before the audit.

resources.title: Preventing Fairness Gerrymandering: Auditing and Learning for Subgroup Fairness
resources.abstract: The most prevalent notions of fairness in machine learning fix a small collection of pre-defined groups (such as race or gender), and then ask for approximate parity of some statistic of the classifier (such as false positive rate) across these groups. Constraints of this form are susceptible to fairness gerrymandering, in which a classifier is fair on each individual group, but badly violates the fairness constraint on structured subgroups, such as certain combinations of protected attribute values. We thus consider fairness across exponentially or infinitely many subgroups, defined by a structured class of functions over the protected attributes. We first prove that the problem of auditing subgroup fairness for both equality of false positive rates and statistical parity is computationally equivalent to the problem of weak agnostic learning — which means it is hard in the worst case, even for simple structured subclasses. However, it also suggests that common heuristics for learning can be applied to successfully solve the auditing problem in practice. We then derive an algorithm that provably converges in a polynomial number of steps to the best subgroup-fair distribution over classifiers, given access to an oracle which can solve the agnostic learning problem. The algorithm is based on a formulation of subgroup fairness as a zero-sum game between a Learner (the primal player) and an Auditor (the dual player). We implement a variant of this algorithm using heuristic oracles, and show that we can effectively both audit and learn fair classifiers on a real dataset.

techniques.name: Actionable Recourse Audit
techniques.description: An actionable recourse audit checks whether the people a linear classifier refuses, for example for a loan, a job interview or a public service, could change that decision through actions open to them, and how much they would have to change. The auditor first writes an action set saying which features can change and how: immutable features such as age stay fixed, features such as education level can only rise, and each changeable feature gets bounds and a grid of realistic values. Then, for each refused person in a sample drawn from the population the model will serve, an integer programming solver (optimisation software that searches discrete choices exactly) looks through the permitted actions for the cheapest change that flips the decision, measuring cost as the largest shift, in population percentiles, that the change makes to any one feature, and either returns that action or proves that none exists, which a search that simply fails to find a counterfactual cannot do. The audit reports the share of refused people who have recourse and the distribution of its cost, which can be compared across candidate models or broken down by group, and the same solver can list a refused person's cheapest alternative changes (a 'flipset') for a decision notice. Unlike the Contrastive Explanation Method, which explains one prediction through features that must be present or absent, or Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE), which searches any model for several alternative inputs that would change one decision, the audit works only on linear models but certifies whether any permitted action exists and summarises the answer across a population.

example_use_cases.description: Before launching a linear model that ranks applications to a housing support scheme, a local authority's analytics team audits recourse on last year's applicants, with age and household size fixed. Its report to the scheme's oversight board gives the share of refused applicants who could qualify through changes the scheme expects, such as completing a tenancy course, and how large those changes are, so the board can decide whether to approve the model.

A credit card issuer generates a flipset for each applicant its linear scorecard declines and puts the two cheapest items in the decline letter, for example reducing current debt to a stated amount, together with the other scored features the applicant should keep unchanged, so that following the stated actions would change the decision under the current model.

A lender's model risk committee is shown recourse audits for candidate credit models of almost equal accuracy. It rejects the most accurate, under which some refused applicants had no feasible action because of an 'ever defaulted' feature, adopts a variant that uses recent defaults only, and has the audit re-run each quarter on new applicants, watching younger applicants, who were scarce in the training data.

An employer's analytics team audits its linear screening model for interview invitations and compares the cost of recourse for refused women and men with similar predicted scores. Sex is not a model input, but the cost can still differ by sex. Refused candidates' true suitability is never observed, so the team cannot also match on outcome as the originating study did, and reports any gap with that caveat to its fairness review panel, which decides whether the features need revising.

limitations.description: The proof that no action exists depends on the model being linear, such as logistic regression, a linear support vector machine or a rule set that can be written in linear form. For tree ensembles or neural networks, a local linear approximation can still suggest actions, which then have to be checked on the real model, but a failure to find one proves nothing, so the share of refused people without recourse is no longer a certified figure.

Every conclusion rests on the action set and cost the auditor chooses. Bounds that are too tight make people appear to lack recourse; loose bounds let a model 'provide' recourse only through drastic changes, which shows only as high cost; and the default cost treats a one-percentile change as equally hard in every feature unless someone who knows the domain sets how much harder some changes are.

The search treats features as changing independently unless the auditor adds constraints. Real actions have knock-on effects: raising income can also raise savings, so a listed action may cost more than needed, or may not change the decision once its effects on other features are counted, as Karimi, Schölkopf and Valera showed for recourse methods that ignore causal relations between features.

Recourse is defined for a fixed model. After retraining, an action given in an earlier notice may no longer change the decision, so the audit has to be re-run after each update. An action that changes the prediction need not change the real outcome either: showing a refused applicant how to be approved can lead them into credit they cannot repay.

A flipset lists only the features to change, so a person who also changes an undisclosed feature may still be refused unless the notice says what must stay the same. The originating paper builds flipsets from public credit datasets and does not test whether refused people understand them or can act on them. Owners may also resist publishing flipsets, because many of them together can let others reconstruct the model.

sample_claims.text: Every refused applicant in the audit sample, drawn from last year's applications to the scheme, has at least one action under the agreed action set that would make them eligible under the deployed model.

Under the agreed action set, at least half of the declined applicants in the audit sample have an action that would bring approval while moving no feature by more than 25 percentiles of the applicant population.
Among candidates refused by the screening model with similar predicted scores, the median cost of recourse for women is within five percentile points of that for men.
Each decline letter lists at least one action that would change the decision under the current scorecard, together with the scored features the applicant must keep unchanged.
